### 1420. assistant — 2026-03-06 07:30:28Z

You’re right to call this out. The dot vs underscore difference is not coming from your CLI; it’s coming from tool‑level naming, plus our normalization logic. Here’s what’s actually happening:

Why both exist

1) netconv and skelconv append .S### (dot)

When smoothing is applied, both tools internally append the smoothing token with a dot:

... .S020.vtu
... .S020.vtp

So crop_x..._filament_manifolds_J1a.S020.vtu is the native tool output.

2) Our code normalizes names to _S###

We run everything through sanitize_filename(...), which converts dots inside the stem to underscores.
So the same file becomes:

... _S020.vtu

3) You now have both because they came from different runs

If: - a run created the dot version, and - another run (or our rename) created the underscore version,

they coexist because they’re different filenames.

That’s why you see both:

..._J1a.S020.vtu
..._J1a_S020.vtu

Why this is currently causing confusion

You also have this warning in the log:

[warn] netconv output name mismatch; using ..._S000.vtu instead of ..._S020.vtu

That happens because our strict matching only looks for _S###, but netconv produced .S020, which we ignored, so we fell back to an old _S000 file.

So the dot/underscore mismatch isn’t just cosmetic — it can lead to using the wrong smoothing level.

Summary

  • Dot .S020 = raw tool output
  • Underscore _S020 = normalized/renamed output
  • Seeing both means multiple runs or partial renames.

If you want, I can do one of the following:

  1. Adjust the matcher to accept .S###, then rename it to _S### (so only one remains).
  2. Skip renaming entirely and just use the tool’s native .S### naming.

### 1424. assistant — 2026-03-06 07:54:22Z

Thanks — the failure is exactly because netconv writes .S020 (dot form), and my strict matcher was only accepting _S020.

I’ve now updated the matcher to accept both _S### and .S###:

  • It will find either form, then
  • sanitize_filename() will normalize the dot to underscore, so only one consistent name remains.

This should fix the crash and prevent the wrong file from being selected.

Updated file - scripts/analyze_snapshot.py

If you rerun the workflow now, it should find the .S020 file, normalize it, and proceed without errors.

### 1426. assistant — 2026-03-06 08:04:05Z

You’re hitting the error because persistence_tag sometimes ends up None, so the code expects a filename without the _s3_5_ segment. That makes the strict matcher miss the real file:

crop_x..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a.S020.vtu

I’ve now updated the matcher to handle that case:

✅ What I changed

In scripts/analyze_snapshot.py:

  • If the strict match fails and no persistence tag is available, it now falls back to a safe substring match that still respects the manifold role (and avoids grabbing filament/cluster manifolds).
  • It also accepts both _S### and .S###.

So even if persistence isn’t detected, the file is still found and normalized.

What you should see now

The run should complete, and the dot name will be normalized to underscore:

..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu

If you want, I can also add a debug print of base_name + persistence_tag to make this easier to diagnose next time.

### 1428. assistant — 2026-03-06 08:26:29Z

Thanks — this failure was still because the matcher only used the “exact base_name” and didn’t fall back when that base_name existed but didn’t match the on‑disk filename. I’ve now made the fallback always run when strict matching fails, regardless of whether a persistence tag was found.

What changed

In scripts/analyze_snapshot.py:

  • If strict matching fails, it now always tries a broader search for:
    • _{role}_..._{tag}
    • It still avoids confusing manifolds with filament_manifolds and cluster_manifolds.

This makes it robust to all the dot/underscore variants and oddities.

Next step

Please re‑run the same command again. It should now find:

..._manifolds_J2a.S020.vtu

and normalize it to:

..._manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu

so the pipeline can proceed.

If you want, I can also add a short debug print of: - base_name - expected_name - matched file

so you can see exactly what it picked in the logs.

### 1433. user — 2026-03-10 04:32:22Z

What does the –dump-cluster-manifolds argument actually accomplish? Does it dump cluster manifolds (from and NDnet file)? Or does it dump clusters from skeletons (from and NDskl file)?

### 1434. assistant — 2026-03-10 04:32:37Z

Short answer: --dump-cluster-manifolds tells mse to dump cluster manifolds into an NDnet (via -dumpManifolds <TAG>), and in our pipeline it also triggers an extra export of cluster critical points (maxima) as VTP/VTU for downstream analysis. It does not dump clusters from the NDskl arcs.

More detail: - From NDnet (manifolds): mse ... -dumpManifolds <TAG> writes <prefix>_sX_manifolds_<TAG>.NDnet and then netconv can convert that to VTU. This is the “cluster manifolds” output, and it is often empty for J3a/JE3a after smoothing. - From critical points (maxima): when --dump-cluster-manifolds is set, we also export cluster critical points (maxima) to <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_<TAG>_S000.vtp/.vtu. This is the primary cluster representation used by ndtopo_stats.py.

So the flag does both: it requests a manifolds NDnet from mse, and it triggers the critical‑point (maxima) export for clusters.

### 1435. user — 2026-03-10 04:35:07Z

OK, are the critical points based on NDnet or NDskl files? Or are they coming from the MSC file?

### 1436. assistant — 2026-03-10 04:35:31Z

They come from the NDskl (skeleton), via skelconv -to crits_ascii. We don’t read the MSC directly.

Pipeline-wise: - mse builds the MSC and writes an NDskl (skeleton). - We run skelconv on that NDskl to export crits_ascii. - We then filter type=3 (maxima) to define clusters.

So: not NDnet, not directly MSC, but NDskl-derived (which itself is produced from the MSC).

### 1437. user — 2026-03-10 04:36:14Z

So the critical points are not actually based on manifolds, right? And therefore clusters aren’t either, right?

### 1438. assistant — 2026-03-10 04:36:17Z

Correct. The cluster critical points are not derived from manifolds. They come from the skeleton/MSC critical points (maxima), extracted via skelconv -to crits_ascii on the NDskl.

So: - Clusters (as we use them) = maxima critical points from the MSC/skeleton. - Not from manifold geometry.

### 1445. user — 2026-03-10 05:56:11Z

what is the tag here: –dump-clusters

### 1446. assistant — 2026-03-10 05:56:28Z

It’s just a label for the cluster critical‑points export. Use the same DisPerSE-style tag you want to associate with clusters (e.g., JE3a or J3a) so filenames and batch matching are consistent.

Important details: - The tag does not change which points are exported. We still take all maxima from the skeleton; the tag is only used in naming. - You still need --dump-arcs (or --skel-input) because the critical points are extracted from the NDskl.

Example:

--dump-clusters JE3a

produces: <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_JE3a_S000.vtp/.vtu

### 1447. user — 2026-03-10 05:58:10Z

but since clusers are not manifold based, what is the point of the tag? the JE3a tag is a manifold tag.

### 1448. assistant — 2026-03-10 05:58:19Z

You’re right: the clusters we export are not manifold‑based, so the tag is just a label. It has two purposes:

  1. Filename/organization – it becomes part of the output name:
    <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_<TAG>_S000.vtp/.vtu
  2. Matching in batch workflows – batch_crop_and_clip.py looks for that tag to pick up the right file.

So the tag doesn’t affect the data, only the naming and downstream matching.
Use anything consistent. Recommended options:

  • Keep JE3a (or J3a) if you want continuity with your MSE tagging style.
  • Or use something neutral like maxima or clusters if you want to avoid manifold semantics.

### 1452. assistant — 2026-03-10 06:22:04Z

You’re right that the persistence tag (s3_5) already distinguishes runs. The extra “manifold tag” and the dotted .crits naming come from how DisPerSE tools name their own outputs and from our conversion helpers, not from the physics.

Here’s what’s going on with the specific names you listed:

1) Why ..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu has the extra “manifolds”

That file is created by our unsmoothed conversion step (via ndtopo_stats.py --write-vtk or when we convert NDnet → VTU). The NDnet file is:

crop_..._s3_5_manifolds_J1a.NDnet

When we convert it, we preserve the original stem (..._manifolds_J1a) and append a role label (filament_manifolds) so the VTU name clearly indicates what it represents. That’s why you get:

..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

It’s redundant, but it avoids collisions and makes the role explicit.

If you want shorter names, we can simplify that naming rule.

2) Why the .crits file has dots:

crop_..._s3_5_cluster_critpoints_J3a.S000.a.crits

This filename comes directly from skelconv -to crits_ascii, which uses the DisPerSE convention:

<base>.S000.a.crits

So the dots are not from our code — they’re DisPerSE’s native naming for the ASCII critical‑point dump. We then read that file and write the cleaned outputs:

..._cluster_critpoints_J3a_S000.vtp/.vtu

3) Why you have both _S000 and _S020

  • _S020 files are the smoothed conversions from netconv/skelconv in analyze_snapshot.py.
  • _S000 files are unsmoothed conversions created by ndtopo_stats.py --write-vtk.

So it’s normal to see both when you run both steps.

4) Why the cluster tag is still present

Even though clusters are not manifold‑based, we keep the tag in the name so: - batch scripts can find the right file, and - multiple runs won’t collide.

But you’re right: the tag does not affect the data. It’s purely a label.

If you want, I can: - simplify the filament‑manifold VTU naming, - remove the tag from cluster critical‑point filenames (or make it optional), - or stop writing the .crits file after generating VTP/VTU.

### 1454. assistant — 2026-03-10 06:24:40Z

Because they’re different roles coming from different NDnet sources, and the conversion code only adds a role suffix when it needs to disambiguate.

  • For walls, the NDnet itself already encodes the role in the stem:

    ..._manifolds_J2a.NDnet  →  ..._manifolds_J2a_S000.vtu

    That’s unambiguous: it’s “the manifolds” file, so no extra suffix is added.

  • For filament manifolds, the NDnet also looks like a manifolds file:

    ..._manifolds_J1a.NDnet

    If we converted that to VTU without a role suffix, it would look exactly like a wall manifolds VTU and would collide or be confusing.
    So the converter adds the role label:

    ..._manifolds_J1a  →  ..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

So the “extra words” only show up when the role isn’t obvious from the base stem (filament manifolds, cluster manifolds). Walls are already obvious, so no extra suffix is added.

If you want, I can simplify this naming convention so the filament manifolds VTU is shorter.

  • You could also use the same tag for multiple dumps (e.g., J1a for walls and filament manifolds) — then the filenames would collide.

That’s why the filament‑manifold VTU gets ..._filament_manifolds_... even though the tag differs.

### 1466. assistant — 2026-03-10 08:18:43Z

Here’s what you’re seeing:

1) The two subfolders

These are ParaView multiblock directories.
When batch_clip.py writes a .vtm file, ParaView saves the .vtm plus a sibling folder that contains the referenced blocks.

So you’ll see pairs like: - crop_..._walls_filaments.vtm - crop_..._walls_filaments/
and similarly for the “filament_manifolds_cluster_manifolds” multiblock.

What’s inside the folders?
They contain the actual per‑block VTK pieces referenced by the .vtm file. The .vtm is just a “table of contents”; the folder is the actual data.

2) Why cluster manifold files look empty

Because those “cluster manifolds” are critical points (VTP with points), not surfaces.
If you view them as surfaces or expect geometry thickness, they look empty.

Specific reasons they can look empty: - They are just points, not surfaces/lines. - The slab clip can remove most/all points if none fall inside the slab thickness. - If you open the flattened (*_cluster_manifolds.vtp) without glyphing, the points can be invisible.

Try this in ParaView: - Open *_cluster_manifolds_3d.vtp - Set Representation = Points - Increase Point Size - Or apply Glyph (Sphere)

You should see the points if any fall into the slab.

3) What each “avg.vti” is

Those *_avg.vti files are resampled/averaged 2D grids for each structure (walls/filaments/cluster/filament manifolds).
They’re only used if you want to treat the topology as a density‑like raster; otherwise you can ignore them.

If you want, I can: - stop writing .vtm multiblocks (and the folders), - skip the *_avg.vti grids for non‑density objects, - or stop writing any of the cluster slab outputs unless you explicitly enable them.

### 1469. user — 2026-03-10 08:57:50Z

can you remind me why is the count and mass_sum of manifolds different in the crop topology stats file? for all other topologies the count and mass_sum match.

### 1470. assistant — 2026-03-10 08:57:58Z

Because the count and mass_sum measure different things:

  • count = number of IDs (Delaunay vertices) that fall into the category.
  • mass_sum = sum of the mass scalar on those Delaunay vertices.

So they only “match” numerically if each vertex has mass = 1.
For most categories in your run, mass behaves close to a constant per vertex, so count ≈ mass_sum.
For manifolds, the selected IDs are biased toward higher‑density regions, so the mass per vertex is larger on average, and mass_sum diverges from count.

In short:
Manifold membership is correlated with higher mass values, so mass_sum is larger even though the number of IDs (count) isn’t.

### 1471. user — 2026-03-10 08:59:18Z

can you remind me why is the count and mass_sum of filaments different in the crop topology stats file? for all other topologies the count and mass_sum match. and the mass for all of them is 1.

### 1472. assistant — 2026-03-10 08:59:34Z

It’s because filament IDs include many points that don’t map to any Delaunay vertex, even though mass = 1 for the Delaunay vertices.

In ndtopo_stats.py: - count = number of filament IDs coming from the skeleton (NDskl, via the cell array). - mass_sum = sum of Delaunay mass only for IDs that actually exist in the Delaunay mesh.

Filament skeletons are densely sampled along arcs; many of those samples are interpolated points whose cell IDs don’t correspond to a Delaunay true_index. Those still count toward count, but they don’t contribute to mass_sum, so mass_sum < count.

If you want count to match mass_sum for filaments, use only valid 0‑cell IDs:

--filaments-cell-mode zero

That keeps only exact integer cell IDs (the actual critical points), so every filament ID should map to Delaunay and the sums will line up.

### 1475. user — 2026-03-10 16:45:01Z

in the new table, when the scalar is not a manifold (i.e it is a filament or cluster) the mass is zero. why?

### 1476. assistant — 2026-03-10 16:45:15Z

Because the filament and cluster datasets don’t carry a mass array.

In the new “topology‑scalars” table we read scalars from the topology files themselves:

  • Filaments (from NDskl/VTP) typically only have geometry + cell/IDs and maybe topology_type, not mass.
  • Cluster critical points we create ourselves, and we only write field_value and log_field_value (no mass).

So when the table tries to aggregate mass from those files, there’s nothing to read, and it defaults to 0.

If you want non‑zero mass there, we have a few options: 1. Map mass from Delaunay for filaments/clusters (similar to the main stats table). 2. Populate mass into the topology datasets when we export them (more work, but cleaner). 3. Drop mass from the topology‑scalar table (or only keep scalars that exist).

Tell me which you prefer and I’ll implement it.

### 1488. assistant — 2026-03-12 04:24:29Z

Short answer:

  • .S020 is the filename convention DisPerSE itself uses when you pass -smooth 20 to netconv/skelconv. It inserts the smooth tag with a dot.
  • Our pipeline normalizes that to _S020 so it’s easier to parse/consistently grep, using sanitize_filename() in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py.
    If you still see both forms, it means the dot‑version was produced in a previous run and not cleaned up, or the rename didn’t occur (best‑effort rename can fail silently). The underscore and dot files should be equivalent, but if their sizes differ, they’re likely from different runs (different parameters or older artifacts), not true duplicates from the same run.

Why you see _S000:

  • _S000 is explicit “unsmoothed” output. We create these in the stats/analysis stage (e.g., ndtopo_stats.py uses -smooth 0 when exporting unsmoothed VTKs for the CSVs). These are intentional and separate from the smoothed S020 visualization meshes.

So in practice: - Use *_S020 for smoothed visualization products. - Use *_S000 for unsmoothed/statistical outputs. - If you want only one naming style, we can add a cleanup step that removes .S### variants after renaming, or we can write everything to a clean output directory each run.

If you want me to add an automatic cleanup, say the word and I’ll implement it.

### 1491. assistant — 2026-03-12 04:40:06Z

Here’s what the code does right now:

  • analyze_snapshot.py never writes S000. It only writes smoothed outputs when --netconv-smooth / --skelconv-smooth > 0 (your runs use 20), so it produces only _S020 files.
    See convert_manifolds() / convert_network() in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py — they only append S### when smooth_iters > 0.

  • S000 is only created by ndtopo_stats.py, and only when it is given NDnet/NDskl and --write-vtk is used. That script converts to unsmoothed VTK with -smooth 0 and names it _S000.
    See ensure_vtu_from_ndnet() / ensure_vtp_from_ndskl() in scripts/ndtopo_stats.py.

So if you don’t see any _S000 now, it means one of these is true:

  1. You’re looking at the slab folder (it never writes S000; it writes *_z0_* outputs only).
  2. ndtopo_stats.py didn’t run or ran with VTK inputs (so no conversion).
  3. The --write-vtk conversion step was skipped (not in your current run, but if you ran stats differently).

If you want me to make sure S000 always gets emitted in the crop folder (or never, by cleaning them up), I can adjust that.

The zsh: killed is almost certainly the OS OOM‑killer. The Polars engine loads all per‑point CSVs into memory at once, and 134M rows across multiple columns can easily exceed RAM (even if it worked before — memory pressure varies).

# 2) Split into 4 roughly equal lists

# 3) Run aggregate per part (write to separate subfolders)

### 1534. user — 2026-03-14 21:03:09Z

but what is the downside of streaming?

### 1535. assistant — 2026-03-14 21:03:18Z

The streaming engine is approximate for plots/histograms and some quantile‑based outputs. Specifically:

  • Stats (count, sum, mean, min, max) are exact.
  • Std/variance is exact (computed online).
  • Histograms/quantiles/violin/box are approximate, because streaming only keeps a reservoir sample (default 20,000) to estimate quantiles and bins.

So the downside is less precise distribution shapes and quantiles. If you only care about aggregate counts and means, streaming is fine; if you need accurate tails/quantiles, use Polars or split‑and‑merge.

If you want streaming but with higher precision, we can increase the reservoir sample size (at some memory cost).

### 1541. assistant — 2026-03-15 04:24:30Z

Yes — Polars is much faster, but it needs enough RAM to hold all the per‑point CSVs at once. That’s why it was killed.

If you want Polars speed without OOM, we can:

  1. Split into a few chunks (e.g., 4 or 8) and run Polars on each chunk.
  2. Merge the chunk stats afterward.

This is the best tradeoff: fast, and stable.

If you want, I’ll add a built‑in “chunked polars” mode so you can do:

--engine polars --chunks 4

and it will handle the split + merge automatically.

How can I make Log_{10} follow latex rules so that the {} shows up as a subscript?

### 1580. assistant — 2026-03-15 22:09:18Z

Use Matplotlib’s mathtext: wrap the label in $...$ and use \log_{10}. Example:

ax.set_ylabel(r'$\log_{10}$ Density')
ax.set_title(r'$\log_{10}$ Density distribution by category')

If you want it literally “Log” (capital L) instead of the log symbol:

ax.set_ylabel(r'$Log_{10}$ Density')

The $...$ is what makes the {10} render as a subscript.

### 1610. assistant — 2026-03-16 17:45:45Z

Short answer: delaunay.vtu is produced by running DisPerSE’s delaunay_3D on your particle catalog and then converting the resulting .NDnet to VTK with netconv.

Process flow (from raw snapshot to delaunay.vtu) 1. Load snapshot particles (PartType1) from data/snapdir_XXX. 2. Crop / stride the particles (your --crop-box and --stride). 3. Write NDfield catalog (*_coords_stride*.AND) with particle positions. 4. Build Delaunay tessellation with DisPerSE: - delaunay_3D <coords.AND> -outName <prefix> -outDir <dir> -btype <periodic|...> - Output: <prefix>.NDnet 5. Convert NDnet to VTK: - netconv <prefix>.NDnet -outName <prefix>_delaunay -outDir <dir> -to vtu - Output: <prefix>_delaunay.vtu

In your pipeline This is handled inside scripts/analyze_snapshot.py when --export-delaunay is set (your batch_crop_and_clip.py passes that). The logs show: - Writing *_coords_stride1.AND - Running delaunay_3D - Running netconv to write *_delaunay.vtu

If you want the exact command you can run manually for a given crop, tell me the crop prefix and output dir and I’ll give you the precise commands.

### 1611. user — 2026-03-16 17:47:45Z

does the delaunay 3d step carry out any interpolation? in other words does the tessalation still contain the original particle positions or are there also interpolated positions too?

### 1612. assistant — 2026-03-16 17:47:51Z

No interpolation is performed by delaunay_3D.

It builds a Delaunay tessellation using your input particle positions as the vertices. The resulting .NDnet stores:

  • the original particle coordinates (as vertices)
  • the connectivity (edges/triangles/tetrahedra) between those points
  • any fields assigned at vertices (e.g., field_value, log_field_value, mass)

So the tessellation contains only the original particle positions, not interpolated points. The interpolation happens later only if you explicitly resample to a grid (e.g., in the slab step when you build *.vti).

Short answer: no, a regular grid is not expected for *_delaunay_point_S000.*. Those points should be the original particle positions (plus any boundary/periodic handling), which are irregular.

If you’re seeing a grid, the most likely causes are:

  1. You opened a resampled density grid, not the point cloud.
    The VTI files like *_density_3d.vti or *_density_avg.vti are regular grids and will look perfectly uniform.

  2. You loaded the right file but ParaView is showing a different pipeline output (e.g., a resampled volume or an image).

  3. You’re looking at delaunay_S000.vtu in “Surface” mode, which only shows the boundary of the unstructured grid.
    For point clouds, the representation should be Points (or Point Gaussian) on the *_delaunay_point_S000.vtp/.vtu file.

If you want to sanity‑check that the file itself isn’t a grid, run this quick check (replace the filename):

python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLPolyDataReader

path = "outputs/.../crop_x..._delaunay_point_S000.vtp"
r = vtkXMLPolyDataReader(); r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
poly = r.GetOutput()
pts = np.array([poly.GetPoint(i) for i in range(poly.GetNumberOfPoints())])

for i, axis in enumerate("xyz"):
    vals = np.unique(pts[:, i])
    diffs = np.unique(np.round(np.diff(np.sort(vals)), 6))
    print(axis, "unique:", len(vals), "diffs sample:", diffs[:10])
PY

If you see lots of unique values and many different diffs, it’s not a grid.

### 1621. user — 2026-03-16 19:58:27Z

after i take a box type slice in paraview, i can’t see the contents of the slice or the points inside. why?

### 1622. assistant — 2026-03-16 19:58:49Z

This is usually one of two things:

  1. A slice has zero thickness
    Your point cloud is 0‑D (vertices). A plane slice has zero volume, so it often hits no points and shows empty output.
    Fix: use a box/clip with thickness or a threshold instead of a plane slice.

  2. Clip without “Crinkle Clip” drops points
    For point data, the standard Clip may operate on cells and can return nothing.
    Fix: in the Clip filter, check “Crinkle clip” so it clips points.

Try this in ParaView - Load *_delaunay_point_S000.vtp (or .vtu), set Representation = Points or Point Gaussian, increase point size. - Use Clip → Box, enable “Crinkle clip”, and make sure Inside Out is correct. - Alternatively use Extract Points or Extract Selection with a box.

If you tell me exactly which file and which filter you’re using (Clip vs Slice vs Extract), I can give a precise fix.

Important: --netconv-smooth 0 affects manifolds, not Delaunay. Delaunay uses --delaunay-smooth (default is 0), so unless you changed that before, it’s already unsmoothed.

They’re 1.5×IQR (Tukey). In code:

  • whishi = min(max, q3 + 1.5 * IQR)

So it uses the standard 1.5×IQR rule, clipped to the observed min/max.

### 1658. assistant — 2026-03-18 02:47:15Z

Here’s the current logic as implemented today in aggregate_topology_points.py. It’s entirely driven by the boolean flags in each *_topology_points.csv row:

  • is_wall
  • is_filament
  • is_filament_manifold
  • is_cluster (or is_cluster_manifold if is_cluster isn’t present)

A single point can be assigned to multiple categories. Nothing is “exclusive” unless the condition explicitly says “not”.

Base categories (wall/filament only)

These are always derived from is_wall and is_filament:

  • walls: is_wall
  • filaments: is_filament
  • shared: is_wall AND is_filament
  • wall_only: is_wall AND NOT is_filament
  • filament_only: is_filament AND NOT is_wall
  • unassigned: NOT is_wall AND NOT is_filament

Note: these names are used in the python engine path.
The polars/stream path uses synonyms: shared_walls_filaments, walls_not_filaments, filaments_not_walls instead of shared, wall_only, filament_only.

Filament-manifold (“filmans”) categories

If is_filament_manifold is present:

  • filmans: is_filament_manifold
  • filmans_not_clusters: is_filament_manifold AND NOT is_cluster
  • filmans_only: is_filament_manifold AND NOT is_wall AND NOT is_filament
  • shared_filmans_walls: is_filament_manifold AND is_wall
  • shared_filaments_filmans: is_filament_manifold AND is_filament
  • walls_not_filmans: is_wall AND NOT is_filament_manifold
  • walls_not_filmans_or_clusters: is_wall AND NOT is_filament_manifold AND NOT is_cluster
  • unassigned_walls_filmans: NOT is_wall AND NOT is_filament_manifold
  • unassigned_walls_filmans_clusters: NOT is_wall AND NOT is_filament_manifold AND NOT is_cluster

Cluster categories

If is_cluster (or is_cluster_manifold) is present:

  • clusters: is_cluster
  • clusters_only: is_cluster AND NOT is_wall AND NOT is_filament
  • shared_walls_clusters: is_cluster AND is_wall
  • shared_filaments_clusters: is_cluster AND is_filament
  • walls_not_clusters: is_wall AND NOT is_cluster
  • unassigned_walls_clusters: NOT is_wall AND NOT is_cluster

Important consistency note

The python engine still emits shared, wall_only, filament_only, unassigned, while the polars/stream code uses shared_walls_filaments, walls_not_filaments, filaments_not_walls. That’s why your CSV looks inconsistent.

If you want fully consistent naming, I can normalize these names across all engines in one pass.

### 1684. assistant — 2026-03-18 05:19:08Z

Here’s what the CSV columns mean and which scalar space they’re in.

Columns (for each category)

The file is *_topology_stats.csv. Each row is one category.

  • category
    The category name (e.g., walls, filmans_only, shared_walls_clusters, etc).

  • count
    Number of points that fall into that category.

For each scalar (typically field_value, log_field_value, plus any others in your per‑point CSV), you get:

  • {scalar}_sum
  • {scalar}_mean
  • {scalar}_min
  • {scalar}_q25
  • {scalar}_median
  • {scalar}_q75
  • {scalar}_max
  • {scalar}_std

These stats are computed over the points in that category.

Which log space is used?

  • field_value
    • Normally: raw, no log
    • If you run with --log10-field-value, then field_value is converted to log10 before stats are computed.
    • In that case, the CSV’s field_value_* columns are log10 density.
  • log_field_value
    Always natural log (ln) from the input data.
    It is not affected by --log10-field-value.

So:

Column prefix Meaning
field_value_* raw density (or log10 if --log10-field-value)
log_field_value_* natural log density
